prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- U.S., Turkish and Iraqi leaders all held talks Monday about Kurdish rebels using northern Iraq as a launchpad for cross-border attacks into Turkey. Turkish troops patrol near the border with Iraq on Monday. President Bush chatted by phone with Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan, while separately two senior Iraq national government figures met with the head of the country's Kurdish region. The diplomatic moves came after Turkish warplanes pounded Kurdish separatist targets in northern Iraq on Saturday and Sunday as well as last week. Bush and Erdogan talked about the dangers of the Kurdish separatist rebels along the Turkish-Iraqi border, the White House confirmed. National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe said they discussed their common efforts to fight terrorism, and the importance of the United States, Turkey and Iraq working together to confront the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK. Bush has vowed to help Turkey fight PKK rebels. The PKK has spent two decades fighting for autonomy for Kurds in southeastern Turkey, with some of its attacks launched from inside northern Iraq. The United States and European Union consider the group a terrorist organization. Last week, Turkey's ambassador to the United States, Nabi Sensoy, said his country's maneuvers against Kurdish militant targets in northern Iraq were based on intelligence provided by the United States. In the Kurdish Iraq city of Sulaimaniya, Iraqi President Jalal Talabani, who is Kurdish, and Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, who is Sunni Arab, met with Kurdish Regional Government President Massoud Barzani. Iraqi Kurdish officials, while critical of the PKK, have denounced the Turkish bombing campaign. Last week, Barzani snubbed visiting U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice in protest of the attacks. "We have vehemently condemned the bombardment. The bombing targeted safe and secure areas and innocent people. Several people were either killed or wounded," Barzani said on Monday at a press conference with the others. "We held consultations with President Jalal Talabani and we will continue our consultations with other concerned parties to put an end to these aggressions and put to an end the shelling of villages." The three Iraqi officials also dealt with national unity. They signed a "memorandum of understanding" to deepen relations further with their three parties: Talabani's Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, Barzani's Kurdistan Democratic Party and al-Hashimi's Iraqi Islamic Party, a Sunni Arab entity. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Kathleen Koch, Talia Kayali and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report .

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — U.S., Turkish, and Iraqi leaders held talks Monday about Kurdish rebels using northern Iraq as a launching point for cross-border attacks into Turkey, as Turkish troops patrolled near the Iraqi border.

President Bush spoke by phone with Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan, while, in a separate meeting, two senior Iraqi national government officials held talks with the leader of the country’s Kurdish region.

The diplomatic efforts followed Turkish airstrikes against Kurdish separatist targets in northern Iraq on Saturday and Sunday, as well as the previous week.

The White House confirmed that Bush and Erdogan discussed the threat posed by Kurdish separatist rebels along the Turkish-Iraqi border. National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe said they addressed their shared efforts to combat terrorism and the importance of cooperation among the United States, Turkey, and Iraq in confronting the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, or PKK.

Bush has pledged to help Turkey fight PKK rebels. For two decades, the PKK has fought for autonomy for Kurds in southeastern Turkey, launching some of its attacks from northern Iraq. The United States and the European Union consider the group a terrorist organization.

Last week, Turkey’s ambassador to the United States, Nabi Sensoy, said his country’s operations against Kurdish militant targets in northern Iraq were based on intelligence provided by the United States.

In the Iraqi Kurdish city of Sulaimaniya, Iraqi President Jalal Talabani, who is Kurdish, and Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, who is Sunni Arab, met with Kurdish Regional Government President Massoud Barzani.

Although Iraqi Kurdish officials have criticized the PKK, they have also denounced the Turkish bombing campaign. Last week, Barzani declined to meet with visiting U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice in protest of the attacks.

“We have vehemently condemned the bombardment. The bombing targeted safe and secure areas and innocent people. Several people were either killed or wounded,” Barzani said Monday at a joint news conference.

“We held consultations with President Jalal Talabani, and we will continue our consultations with other concerned parties to put an end to these aggressions and to the shelling of villages.”

The three Iraqi officials also addressed national unity. They signed a “memorandum of understanding” aimed at further deepening relations among their three parties: Talabani’s Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, Barzani’s Kurdistan Democratic Party, and al-Hashimi’s Iraqi Islamic Party, a Sunni Arab organization.

E-mail to a friend.

CNN’s Kathleen Koch, Talia Kayali, and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — On Monday, officials from the United States, Turkey and Iraq held discussions about Kurdish militants who use northern Iraq as a base for raids across the border into Turkey, as Turkish soldiers patrolled near the Iraqi frontier.

President George W. Bush spoke by telephone with Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan. In a separate meeting, two senior Iraqi national officials held talks with the leader of Iraq’s Kurdish region.

The diplomatic activity followed Turkish airstrikes against Kurdish separatist positions in northern Iraq on Saturday and Sunday, as well as during the previous week.

The White House confirmed that Bush and Erdogan discussed the threat posed by Kurdish separatist fighters along the Turkey-Iraq border. National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe said the conversation covered joint counterterrorism efforts and the need for the United States, Turkey and Iraq to cooperate against the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, known as the PKK.

Bush has promised U.S. assistance to Turkey in its campaign against the PKK. For approximately 20 years, the organization has fought for Kurdish autonomy in southeastern Turkey, sometimes carrying out attacks from bases in northern Iraq. Both the United States and the European Union classify the PKK as a terrorist group.

Nabi Sensoy, Turkey’s ambassador to the United States, said the previous week that Turkish operations targeting Kurdish militants in northern Iraq had relied on intelligence supplied by Washington.

Meanwhile, in the Iraqi Kurdish city of Sulaimaniya, Iraqi President Jalal Talabani, a Kurd, and Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, a Sunni Arab, met with Massoud Barzani, president of the Kurdistan Regional Government.

Although Iraqi Kurdish leaders have criticized the PKK, they have also condemned Turkey’s bombing operations. The previous week, Barzani declined to meet visiting U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice as a protest against the strikes.

Speaking at a joint news conference Monday, Barzani said the bombardment had been strongly denounced because it struck peaceful, secure locations and harmed civilians, leaving several people dead or injured. He added that he had consulted Talabani and would continue discussions with other relevant parties in an effort to stop both the attacks and the shelling of villages.

The three Iraqi leaders also addressed national reconciliation. They signed a memorandum of understanding intended to strengthen cooperation among their political organizations: Talabani’s Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, Barzani’s Kurdistan Democratic Party and al-Hashimi’s Iraqi Islamic Party, which represents Sunni Arabs.

CNN’s Kathleen Koch, Talia Kayali and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to the report. The original article also included an option to email it to a friend.
outputs.L3:
U.S., Turkish, and Iraqi leaders held talks over the presence of Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) rebels in northern Iraq, which they were using as a base to launch attacks into Turkey. President George W. Bush and Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan stressed the need for close cooperation among the United States, Turkey, and Iraq to counter the group and prevent further cross-border violence.

As part of its campaign against the PKK, Turkey carried out airstrikes on Kurdish separatist targets in northern Iraq. The operations reportedly relied on intelligence provided by the United States, reflecting increased security coordination between Washington and Ankara.

The PKK had waged an armed struggle for Kurdish autonomy in southeastern Turkey for approximately two decades. Both the United States and the European Union designated the group as a terrorist organization.

Iraqi Kurdish officials also criticized the PKK and its activities. However, they strongly condemned Turkey’s bombing campaign, arguing that the strikes harmed civilians and targeted areas that had previously been considered secure. Their response highlighted the tension between opposition to the PKK and concern over the humanitarian and regional consequences of Turkish military action.
outputs.L4:
U.S., Turkish, and Iraqi officials pursued a series of coordinated talks aimed at preventing fighters from the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, or PKK, from using bases in northern Iraq to carry out attacks across the border into Turkey. The discussions reflected a shared concern that continued PKK activity could destabilize the border region, strain relations between Ankara and Baghdad, and threaten the security of Iraq’s Kurdish-administered north.

At the same time, Turkey continued airstrikes against suspected PKK positions in northern Iraq. Reports indicated that some operations may have been supported by intelligence supplied by the United States, which, like Turkey, considers the PKK a terrorist organization. Turkish authorities defended the strikes as necessary measures against militants responsible for attacks inside Turkey.

The diplomatic effort nevertheless revealed significant disagreements over how to confront the group. Iraqi Kurdish leaders condemned the Turkish bombings, saying they had caused civilian casualties and struck areas that had previously been considered secure. They warned that cross-border military action could disrupt local communities, undermine stability, and infringe on Iraqi sovereignty.

Thus, although the United States, Turkey, Iraq, and the Kurdish regional authorities broadly opposed the PKK’s armed campaign, they remained divided over tactics. Ankara emphasized its right to act against cross-border threats, while Iraqi and Kurdish officials pressed for restraint, greater coordination, and measures that would protect civilians and respect Iraqi territory.
outputs.L5: **WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Turkish officials held talks in Washington this week as the United States and Turkey sought to strengthen cooperation on regional security, trade, and diplomatic issues. Discussions focused on NATO priorities, developments in the Middle East, and efforts to resolve long-standing disagreements between the two allies. Both sides described the meetings as constructive, while acknowledging that further negotiations would be needed.

**Turkish airstrikes on Kurdish rebels fuel tension along Iraqi border**

**ERBIL, Iraq —** Tensions rose along the Turkish-Iraqi border after Turkish warplanes attacked positions held by Kurdish militants in northern Iraq, threatening a fragile peace process and raising fears that civilians could be drawn into renewed fighting.

Turkey said the strikes targeted camps and shelters used by the Kurdistan Workers Party, or PKK, in the mountainous Qandil region. The PKK has waged an insurgency against the Turkish state for greater Kurdish rights and is designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union.

The attacks followed renewed violence inside Turkey and marked a sharp reversal in Ankara’s efforts to end a conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people since 1984.

Massoud Barzani, then president of Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan Regional Government, urged both sides to step back from confrontation.

“The peace process is the best way to resolve problems, and war benefits no side,” Barzani said in a statement after speaking with Turkish officials.

Barzani also called on the PKK to remove its fighters from populated areas and from the Kurdistan Region, saying their presence risked exposing local residents to Turkish bombardment.

“The PKK should withdraw its forces from the Kurdistan Region so that civilians are not made victims of this war,” he said.

The strikes put the regional government in a difficult position. Iraqi Kurdish leaders maintain close economic and political ties with Turkey, including extensive energy trade, but many people in the region sympathize with Kurdish aspirations across the border. The KRG is separate from the PKK and has repeatedly said its territory should not be used to launch attacks on neighboring countries.

Iraq’s central government protested Turkish military operations carried out without Baghdad’s approval, describing them as a violation of Iraqi sovereignty. Turkish officials countered that the campaign was an act of self-defense against militants operating from bases beyond Turkey’s borders.

Residents of border villages reported hearing aircraft and explosions in remote mountain areas. The number of casualties could not be independently confirmed.

The escalation raised concern that fighting could displace villagers and further destabilize northern Iraq, where Kurdish forces were also battling Islamic State militants. Barzani urged Ankara and the PKK to revive negotiations, warning that a military solution would deepen the region’s already complex conflicts.
